newsitem.title: USA: Epitope unit erred on berries' source.
newsitem.headline: Epitope unit erred on berries' source.

text.p: Epitope Inc said Wednesday its Andrew and Williamson Sales Co unit had inaccurately described some of the strawberries linked with an occurrence of Hepatitis A in Michigan schools as having been grown and processed in the U.S.
It also said Fred Williamson had resigned as president and chief executive of the unit.
Andrew and Williamson has begun recalling the strawberries, shipped to distributors for institutional use in six states.
According to Epitope, the unit said the strawberries were grown in U.S., as required by the U.S. Department of Agriculture School Lunch Program.
In fact, the berries were grown in Mexico and processed in the U.S., Epitope said in a statement.

"We have notified the USDA of our concern with regard to this matter and have today accepted the resignation of Fred Williamson, president and chief executive officer of A&W," said Adolph Ferro, president and chief executive of Epitope.
"This whole incident just reflects the fact that Epitope made a miscalculation when they got into the agriculture business with this acquisition," said one analyst.
"Their main business is diagnostic and their main product is an HIV diagnostic test," the analyst said.
For the year ended September 30, 1996, Epitope reported a net loss of $1.4 million, compared with a net loss of $18.5 million in the previous year.

Beaverton, Oregon-based Epitope completed the acquisition of Andrew and Williamson in mid-December. In the year ended September 30, 1996, A&W had sales of $62.5 million and pre-tax net income of $1.3 million.
